10 linked to an investment account and automatically transfers funds when the balance

19

20

21

23

24

27

 5 interest rate.

 7

 9 as their customers’ agents in establishing and maintaining the Program. The Account

 5         6.     Defendants breached their fiduciary duties when it placed their

 2         13. Defendant Wells Fargo & Company is headquartered at 420 Montgomery

 5

     “RIA” that offers brokerage and investment advisory services to its nationwide

27                             FACTUAL BACKGROUND
28

30
                                              6
31

 1          A. Defendants’ Customer Relationship and Contractual Duties

 2         15.     The relationship between Defendants and their customers, including
 3
     Plaintiff, is set forth in the Account Agreement. The Account Agreement
 4
     incorporates by reference “applicable disclosure documents related to your Account
 5

 6 (‘Account Disclosures’) and any additions, amendments, or supplements to such

 7
     documents,” as well as other agreements “which may be applicable to a particular
 8
     feature, program, account, or service related to your account.”
 9

10         16.     One of the Account Disclosures is the Cash Sweep Program
11
     Disclosure Statement (“Program Disclosure”). The Program Disclosure state that
12
     Defendants act as customers’ agent in operating the Program:
13

14         Wells Fargo Advisors will act as your agent in establishing and
           maintaining the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs, including making
15         deposits to and withdrawals from the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs.
16         Your first deposit into the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep or Expanded
           Bank Deposit Sweep will constitute your appointment of Wells Fargo
17
           Advisors as your agent in connection with the Standard Bank Deposit
18         Sweep or Expanded Bank Sweep.
19
           17.     By entering a custodial and agency relationship with Plaintiff and
20
     members of the putative Class, Defendants assumed fiduciary duties including the
21

22 duty of loyalty, the duty of care, the duty to act in good faith, the duty of full and fair

23 disclosures, and the duty to make prudent investment recommendations. These

24
     fiduciary duties are meant to always ensure Defendants act with integrity and in the
25

26 best interests of the client.

27         18.     Defendant’s fiduciary duties to as broker-dealers are described in
28

30
                                                7
31
             Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1     Filed 10/14/24   Page 8 of 37




 1 Regulation Best Interest (Reg. BI) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which

 2 requires them to act in the best interests of the retail customer at the time a

 3
     recommendation is made. Reg. BI applies to retail investors, i.e., natural persons, or
 4
     their legal representatives, who receive recommendations primarily for personal,
 5

 6 family, or household purposes. 17 C.F.R. § 240.15l-1(b)(1).

 7
           19.     Reg. BI obligates broker-dealers, when making an investment
 8
     recommendation, to meet four core obligations: Disclosure (providing certain
 9

10 prescribed disclosure before or at the time of recommendation, about the

11 recommendation and the relationship between the retail customer and the broker-

12
     dealer); Care (exercising reasonable diligence, care, and skill in making the
13

14 recommendation); Conflicts of Interest (establishing, maintaining, and enforcing

15 policies and procedures reasonably designed to address conflicts of interest); and

16
     Compliance (establishing, maintaining, and enforcing policies and procedures
17

18 reasonably designed to achieve compliance with Reg BI).

19         20.     Another Account Disclosure is Defendants’ “Regulation Best Interest
20
     Disclosure (for Retail Customers Under 17 CFR 240.151-1).” Through this
21
     agreement, Defendants acknowledge that they are bound by RegBi’s obligations.
22

23         21.     Defendants’ fiduciary duties are also reflected in their Code of
24
     Conduct.                                                                          See
25
     https://www08.wellsfargomedia.com/assets/pdf/about/corporate/code-of-
26

27 conduct.pdf.

28         22.     As its customers’ agent and pursuant to its contractual obligations,
30
                                               8
31
             Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC     Document 1     Filed 10/14/24   Page 9 of 37




 1 Defendants are required to act in their best interests and not put their own personal

 2 gain ahead of their clients.

 3
            B. Defendants’ Bank Deposit Sweep Program
 4
           23.     A “sweep program” is a “service provided by a broker or dealer where
 5

 6 it offers to its customer the option to automatically transfer free credit balances in

 7 the securities account of the customer to either a money market mutual fund product

 8
     as described in § 270.2a-7 or an account at a bank whose deposits are insured by the
 9

10 Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation.” See 17 CFR 240.15c3-3(a)(17).

11         24.     Sweep deposits play a pivotal role as a capital source for banks,
12
     empowering them to utilize these deposits for various corporate purposes. This
13
     includes activities such as making loans or investing in government securities. The
14

15 disparity between the interest rate paid and the interest rate earned by a bank on those

16 deposits is commonly referred to as the net interest margin (“NIM”). See also

17
     Account Agreement (“the profitability of the banks in the Bank Deposit Sweep
18

19
     Programs, including Affiliated Banks, is determined in large part by the difference

20 or ‘spread’ between the interest they pay on deposits, and the interest or other income

21
     they earn on loans, investments, and other assets.”).
22
           25.     Profits earned by brokerage firms from their sweep programs are
23

24 based on their agreements with the affiliated bank which generally provide

25 compensation based on the average daily deposits at the affiliated bank, with total

26
     compensation generally based on the Federal Funds rate plus basis points.
27
           26.     During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Federal Funds rate (an interest
28

30
                                               9
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1     Filed 10/14/24   Page 10 of 37




 1 rate set by the Federal Open Market Committee which banks use to lend each other

 2 money) was so low that the earned interest on cash sweep would be very low. Before

 3
     and after the pandemic, however, the Federal Funds rate was substantially higher.
 4
     For example, from 2022 to 2024, the Federal Funds rate rose from an average yield
 5

 6 of 1.68% in 2022 to 5.03% in 2023 to 5.44% in 2024.

 7         27.     When the Federal Fund rate rose beginning in 2022, banks increased
 8
     yields and so brokerages should have been able to negotiate higher rates of return on
 9

10
     uninvested cash from affiliated banks. Unfortunately, that has not been the case with

11 some firms such as Wells Fargo. Instead, WFA places sweep deposits with Affiliated

12
     Banks that it negotiates with to pay less than reasonable interest rates to customers
13
     and more money for itself.
14

15         28.     The deposit accounts in the Program have very low rates of return.

16 Throughout 2022 and at least through April 2023, the interest rates paid to customers

17
     with cash sweep deposits were paltry: from .05% to approximately .30%.
18
           29.     The SEC, in its Staff Bulletin: Standards of Conduct for Broker-
19

20 Dealers and Investment Advisers Conflicts of Interest, issued August 3, 2022,

21 emphasized that “cash sweep programs” are a “common source[ ] of conflicts of

22
     interest.” See https://www.sec.gov/tm/iabd-staff-bulletin-conflicts-interest.
23

24         30.     By default, Defendants primarily assign its customers to one of two

25 different cash sweep programs.

26
           31.     Under the Program, uninvested cash balances will automatically
27
     sweep daily into interest bearing deposit accounts set by Defendants following the
28

30
                                              10
31
             Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC     Document 1     Filed 10/14/24   Page 11 of 37




 1 day of deposit and with the banks selected by Defendants.

 2          32.     The Account Agreement states that Wells Fargo assumes “no
 3
     obligation to seek or negotiate interest rates in excess of any reasonable rate of
 4

 5 interest the Affiliated Banks are willing to credit,” thereby creating an obligation, as

 6 an agent and fiduciary of its clients, to negotiate a reasonable rate of interest, which

 7
     Wells Fargo purposely failed to do so it could earn more revenue for itself.
 8

 9 (Emphasis added).

10          33.     For the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep, the cash is only swept into
11
     deposit accounts with Affiliated Banks.
12

13          34.     For the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep, the uninvested cash is swept

14 into an interest-bearing deposit account with one of five banks including Wells Fargo

15
     Affiliated Banks and unaffiliated Banks. Importantly, “for retirement accounts in the
16

17 Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep, the ordering of the sweep is always Affiliated Banks

18 first,         and      then      unaffiliated       Program         Banks.”        See
19
     https://www.wellsfargoclearingservicesllc.com/pdf/program-banksFC.pdf
20

21 (emphasis added).

22          35.     The Standard Bank Deposit Sweep and Expanded Bank Deposit
23
     Sweep are separate products from Wells Fargo’s investment advisory services and
24

25 are optional.

26          36.     The interest rates on Wells Fargo’s cash sweep accounts were set by
27
     Wells Fargo’s Affiliated Banks in consultation with Wells Fargo and it failed to
28

30
                                               11
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1      Filed 10/14/24    Page 12 of 37




 1 negotiate a reasonable interest rate on behalf of its customers when these rates were

 2 set.

 3
           37.    Additionally, under the Program, Unaffiliated Banks were required to
 4

 5 set their interest rates at the same rate as the Affiliated Banks.

 6        38.      Defendants acknowledge that their arrangement with the Affiliate
 7
     Banks is a conflict of interest that must be disclosed. For example, the Account
 8
     Agreement discloses that WFA “has a conflict of interest as a result of” the benefits
 9

10 it receive from the Program “because it and its affiliates benefit financially from the

11 Bank Deposit Sweep Program and Wells Fargo Advisors choose include these

12
     options, instead of selecting other cash investment options that would not generate
13

14 these financial benefits, and that may pay you higher rates of interest.”

15         39.     Defendants as their customers’ agent and exercise discretion with
16
     respect to the Program. Defendants exercised this discretion in bad faith to the
17
     detriment of their customers.
18

19         40.     The Program primarily benefited Defendants at the expense of their
20 customers.

21
           41.     Defendants enter transactions by which it establishes and pays
22

23
     unreasonably low interest rates to its customers in the Program. In contrast to the

24 unreasonably low returns Defendants pays their customers, Defendants shifts to their

25
     Affiliated Banks a substantial portion of the beneficial returns on its customers’ cash
26

27
     that would otherwise constitute its customary compensation in connection with the

28 Program.

30
                                               12
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC       Document 1     Filed 10/14/24    Page 13 of 37




 1         42.      Defendants admit that by keeping the interest rates in Plaintiff and

 2 Class members’ deposit accounts lower, it earns a higher profit.

 3
           43.      Through their operation of the Program, Defendants engage in self-
 4

 5
     dealing, creating a profit center that benefits only them, to the financial detriment of

 6 their customers.

 7
            C. Defendants’ Disclosures to Its Customers Regarding the Program
 8             Contained Material Misrepresentations and Omissions
 9
           44.      Defendants’ disclosures contain material misrepresentations and
10
     omissions regarding the Program.
11

12         45.      The Program Disclosure states: “The rates of return for the sweep
13
     options vary over time. Current rates can be obtained from your investment
14
     professional, by calling the general inquiries phone number listed on the front of
15

16 your          account      statement,      or      found       on       our       website
17
     at https://www.wellsfargoadvisors.com/cashsweep.”         (Emphasis     added).    This
18
     statement is misleading because it suggests that if interest rates for consumers rise
19

20 (for example, through the federal funds rate), they will go up concurrently for the

21
     client, when in truth, Defendants kept rates artificially low, regardless of market
22
     conditions. These disclosures are misleading by claiming that the interest rates paid
23

24 to customers is a function of economic and market conditions. In fact, the interest

25
     rates on the Program are significantly below market rates and are not reasonably tied
26
     to any economic or market condition.
27

28         46.      The Program Disclosure states: “The rates of interest paid on affiliated
30
                                               13
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1      Filed 10/14/24   Page 14 of 37




 1 Program Bank deposits will be periodically set and re-set the affiliated Program

 2 Banks in consultation with Wells Fargo Advisors. Wells Fargo Advisors will direct

 3
     and otherwise cause the unaffiliated Program Banks participating in the Expanded
 4

 5 Bank Deposit Sweep program to credit interest on their respective deposits at the

 6 same rate then being credited by the affiliated Program Banks.” This statement is

 7
     misleading because it suggests that if interest rates for consumers rise (for example,
 8

 9 through the federal funds rate), they will go up concurrently for the client, when in

10 truth, Defendants kept rates artificially low, regardless of market conditions. These

11
     disclosures are misleading by claiming that the interest rates paid to customers is a
12

13 function of economic and market conditions. In fact, the interest rates on the Program

14 are significantly below market rates and are not reasonably tied to any economic or

15
     market condition.
16

17         47.     The Program Disclosure states: “The interest rates on the Standard

18 Bank Deposit Sweep and Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep will reflect the amounts

19
     that the Program Banks credit to their respective deposit accounts, net of the fees
20

21 paid to Wells Fargo Advisors and others, as set forth below under ‘Benefits to Wells

22 Fargo Advisors and Others.’” (Emphasis added). This statement is misleading

23
     because it fails to disclose that WFA received excessive fees because of its conflicted
24

25 relationship with the Affiliated Banks. This is a material omission of facts that

26 customers would have found important in decided whether to use Defendants as their

27
     investment advisor.
28

30
                                               14
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1    Filed 10/14/24   Page 15 of 37




 1         48.     Defendants never disclose the interest rates that their Deposit

 2 Accounts could have earned if their customers’ sweep funds had been invested in

 3
     comparable accounts with non-affiliated banks. This is a material omission of facts
 4
     that customers would have found important in decided whether to use Defendants as
 5

 6 their investment advisor.

 7          D. Defendants Know the Program Must Provide a Reasonable Rate of
 8             Interest.

 9         49.     Defendants knew or should have known that it has a duty to offer
10
     retirement accounts investors a reasonable rate of interest. This knowledge flows not
11

12 only from the contractual language and fiduciary duties discussed above, but also

13 from additional duties imposed on Defendants by law.

14
           50.     For example, Defendants’ Roth Individual Retirement Account
15

16 Disclosure Statement and Custodial agreement (“Roth Agreement”) states that

17 Defendants must not engage in “a prohibited transaction”—“any improper use of

18
     your Roth IRA by you, your beneficiary or any disqualified person” —because it
19

20 could result in the loss of the IRA’s tax-favored status. The Roth Agreement advises

21 that “to learn more about prohibited transactions and who is a disqualified person,

22
     refer to IRS Publication 590.” IRS Publication 590 explains that “disqualified
23

24 persons include your fiduciary,”—i.e., Defendants.

25
           51.     Section 4975 of the IRC (entitled “Tax on Prohibited Transactions”),
26
     applies to IRAs generally, including Plaintiff’s IRA. See 26 U.S.C. §4975(e)(1)(B)
27

28 (defining “plan” to include “an individual retirement account described in [IRC]

30
                                              15
31
            Case 3:25-cv-01968-VC      Document 1     Filed 10/14/24   Page 16 of 37




 1 Section 408(a)”). IRC § 4975(c)(1)(B) defines as a “prohibited transaction” the

 2 “lending of money or other extension of credit between a plan [i.e., an individual

 3
     IRA] and a disqualified person.” A “disqualified person,” under Section 4975(e)(2)
 4

 5 includes, among others, “a fiduciary” and “a person providing services to the plan.”

 6         52.     Defendants and the Bank are “disqualified person[s]” under Section
 7
     4975(e)(2) and, therefore, the sweep agreement for retirement accounts between
 8

 9 Plaintiff and Defendants are “prohibited transaction[s]” under § 4975(c)(1)(B).

10         53.     IRC § 4975(d)(4) provides several “exemptions,” or safe harbors, for
11
     otherwise “prohibited transactions,” one of which is “the investment of all or part of
12

13 a plan’s assets in deposits which bear a reasonable interest rate in a bank or similar

14 financial institution.” (Emphasis added).

15
           54.     Section 4975 recognizes that related party transactions into which
16

17 customers are defaulted (such as Defendants’ Program) can offer interest rates that

18 may become unfairly lowered due to inherent conflicts of interest. Accordingly,

19
     conflicted transactions such as affiliated entity cash sweeps are required to pay a
